mu-b57b3d1a.stem: While the patient stands on the right leg, the left side of the pelvis drops (positive Trendelenburg sign). Where is the lesion?
mu-b57b3d1a.explanation: When standing on one leg, gluteus medius and minimus of that side keep the pelvis level. In right superior gluteal nerve palsy, standing on the right leg lets the unsupported left pelvis drop. When walking the patient compensates by leaning the trunk towards the paralysed side.

mu-70332bc2.stem: Which is the safe area for intramuscular injection into the gluteal region, and why?
options: Upper inner quadrant; because it is away from the superior gluteal nerve
Upper outer quadrant; because it is away from the sciatic nerve
Lower outer quadrant; because it is away from the large vessels
Exact centre; because the muscle layer is thinnest
Lower inner quadrant; because the muscle mass is thickest
mu-70332bc2.explanation: The sciatic nerve emerges in the lower inner part of the gluteal region, below piriformis, and descends between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity. The upper outer quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) is therefore preferred.

mu-0d58bed8.stem: Which nerve passes through the part of the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis (suprapiriform)?
mu-0d58bed8.explanation: Only the superior gluteal nerve and the superior gluteal artery and vein pass through the suprapiriform opening. Through the infrapiriform opening pass the inferior gluteal nerve, sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal artery and the nerves to the short rotators.

mu-7ffea930.stem: In a patient with right lower quadrant pain, pain increases when he lies on his left side and the right hip is passively extended. On which muscle does this suggest the inflamed appendix lies?
mu-7ffea930.explanation: Psoas sign: an inflamed retrocaecal appendix touches the fascia of psoas; extending the hip stretches the muscle and increases the pain. The obturator sign is pain on flexion and internal rotation of the hip in pelvic appendicitis.

mu-119f3442.stem: What are the nerve supply and action of tensor fasciae latae?
options: Inferior gluteal nerve – extends the hip
Superior gluteal nerve – tenses the iliotibial tract and flexes and abducts the hip
mu-119f3442.explanation: TFL is supplied by the same nerve as gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve). Through the iliotibial tract it also stabilises the outer side of the knee; excessive tightness leads to iliotibial band syndrome.

mu-6c36a36f.stem: Which is the longest muscle in the body, also known as the 'tailor's muscle'?
mu-6c36a36f.explanation: Sartorius arises from the ASIS, crosses the thigh and attaches to the medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus). It flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip and flexes the knee (cross-legged sitting). It is supplied by the femoral nerve and forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.

mu-42b3e48d.stem: Which head of quadriceps femoris both flexes the hip and extends the knee?
mu-42b3e48d.explanation: Because rectus femoris arises from the AIIS and the upper rim of the acetabulum it also crosses the hip joint; the three vasti arise only from the femur and only extend the knee. All of quadriceps is supplied by the femoral nerve.

mu-f5216881.stem: With which nerve is the 'hamstring part' of the doubly innervated adductor magnus supplied?
options: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve
Fibular part of the sciatic nerve
Posterior branch of the obturator nerve
mu-f5216881.explanation: The adductor part of adductor magnus is supplied by the obturator nerve, the hamstring part arising from the ischial tuberosity by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. The opening between the two parts is the adductor hiatus.

mu-3c7631f1.stem: Which structures pass through the adductor hiatus to reach the popliteal fossa?
options: Anterior branch of the obturator nerve
mu-3c7631f1.explanation: After following the adductor canal, the femoral artery and vein pass through the opening in adductor magnus and become the popliteal artery and vein. The saphenous nerve leaves the canal and turns to the medial side of the knee without entering the hiatus.

mu-e001f998.stem: Which of the following is NOT found in the adductor (Hunter's) canal?
mu-e001f998.explanation: The adductor canal lies under sartorius, between vastus medialis and the adductors; the femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis pass through it. The great saphenous vein is a superficial vein running in the superficial fascia.

mu-ec430720.stem: Which muscle of the hamstring group is supplied by the common fibular nerve?
mu-ec430720.explanation: Most hamstring muscles receive the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur (linea aspera), is not a true hamstring and is supplied by the fibular part.

mu-0bd4523e.stem: To which muscles do the tendons forming the pes anserinus belong?
mu-0bd4523e.explanation: The three tendons join on the upper medial surface of the tibia in a goose-foot shape and are supplied by three different nerves: sartorius (femoral nerve), gracilis (obturator nerve), semitendinosus (sciatic nerve–tibial part). Inflammation of the bursa beneath them is pes anserinus bursitis.

mu-45908f38.stem: Which thigh muscle may be supplied by both the femoral nerve and the obturator nerve?
mu-45908f38.explanation: Pectineus is supplied mainly by the femoral nerve and often also by the obturator (or accessory obturator) nerve; it is therefore regarded as a transitional muscle between the anterior and medial compartments.

mu-2700c78e.stem: Which muscle forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle?
mu-2700c78e.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded above by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the medial border of sartorius and medially by the medial border of adductor longus. Its floor is formed by iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus; it contains, from lateral to medial, the femoral nerve, artery, vein and lymphatics.
